block.label: READING · PLAGUE SCARE IN SIBERIA
block.html:
The USA has raised concerns after a worker at a plague research laboratory in Siberia died. Some newspapers suspect that she died after coming into contact with plague bacteria. The 28-year-old worker died after developing severe pneumonia. Local reports say she may have broken a test tube containing plague bacteria. Dozens of hospital workers have been quarantined. Officials are monitoring people who were in contact with the woman who died. Russia has said the woman’s death was from “pneumonia of an unknown origin” and not plague. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said there was no “cause for alarm”. He said officials should “keep an eye on it”.

Pneumonic plague can be deadly. It attacks the lungs and can cause death 18 to 24 hours after symptoms begin. It is highly contagious, so it can spread quickly. It can move from person to person through the air when an infected person coughs or sneezes. The disease can be treated with antibiotics. However, antibiotics work best when they are given as soon as symptoms appear. Pneumonic plague is different from COVID-19, which is caused by a virus and not a bacterium. COVID-19 spreads much more easily around the world than plague. Microbiologist Dr Simon Clarke told the BBC: “Pneumonic plague can spread from person to person, and that is why there is the concern around this.”

IELTS tip: skim the whole text in 2 minutes first, then read again to answer the questions.

block.label: PHRASAL VERBS · OUTBREAKS & ILLNESS
block.html:
Phrasal verbs make you sound natural, and IELTS examiners notice them (Lexical Resource). Learn them as a story:
• A disease breaks out. People come down with it and pass it on.
• Patients try to fight it off. With luck, they pull through.
• Officials look into the case, track down contacts, shut down the lab and rule out some causes. Sometimes governments cover things up.
• In history, diseases have wiped out whole cities, and some have never completely died out.

Separable (the object can go in the middle): pass it on, track them down, shut it down, rule it out, cover it up, fight it off, wipe them out, carry it out.
With a pronoun, the middle is obligatory: pass it on ✓ — pass on it ✗
Not separable: look into it, come down with it. No object: break out, die out, pull through.

rows: start suddenly (a disease, a war, a fire)
start to suffer from an illness
Infected people can pass it on by coughing.
Her body couldn’t fight off the infection.
The Black Death wiped out a third of Europe.
They have tracked down everyone she met.
say that something is not possible
The lab carries out research on bacteria.

block.label: GRAMMAR · PRESENT PERFECT vs PAST PERFECT
block.html:
Present Perfect (have / has + past participle) connects the past to now. The news loves it, because the result matters today:
The USA has raised concerns. Dozens of hospital workers have been quarantined.

Past Perfect (had + past participle) is the past of the past: something that happened before another moment in the past:
When she arrived at the hospital, she had already developed severe pneumonia.
Officials discovered that she had broken a test tube.

Quick test: does it connect to now (“until now”, “so far”)? → Present Perfect. Did it happen before another past moment (“by then”, “before that”)? → Past Perfect. A finished time (in 1347, yesterday)? → Past Simple.

rows: ever, never, just, already, yet, so far, since, for, recently
by the time, before, after, when, already, until then

block.label: IELTS SPEAKING · PARTS 1, 2 & 3
block.html: Part 1: short, natural answers (2–3 sentences). Part 2: 1 minute to prepare, then speak for 2 minutes. Part 3: give opinions, reasons and examples.

cats.name: Part 1 · Health
qs: How often do you get ill?
What do you do to stay healthy?
Do you trust health information you find online?
Have you ever been to hospital?
Do you prefer going to the doctor or treating yourself at home?

cats.name: Part 2 · Cue cards
qs: Describe a time when you were ill. You should say: when it happened, what illness you had, how you felt, and explain how you got better.
Describe a piece of news that surprised you. You should say: what it was, where you heard it, how people reacted, and explain why it surprised you.
Describe a scientist or doctor you admire. You should say: who this person is, what they have done, how you know about them, and explain why you admire them.

cats.name: Part 3 · Discussion
qs: Should governments be allowed to put people in quarantine against their will?

Do the media cause unnecessary panic about health issues?

block.label: DEBATE · DEVIL'S ADVOCATE
block.html: Draw a statement and a side. Defend that side for 1 minute, even if you disagree. Use at least one Present Perfect and one phrasal verb.
lines: Laboratories that work with dangerous diseases should be shut down.
Governments should be able to force people into quarantine.
The media exaggerate health scares to sell news.
Vaccines should be compulsory for everyone.
Countries should share all information about outbreaks immediately.
Scientific research is worth any risk.

block.label: HOMEWORK · IELTS WRITING TASK 2
block.html:
Some people think that laboratories working with dangerous diseases should be closed down because the risks are too high. Others believe this research is essential to protect humanity. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

Write at least 250 words in 40 minutes.
• Introduction: paraphrase the question and give your position.
• Body 1: why some people want these labs shut down (accidents, diseases that people pass on, governments that cover things up).
• Body 2: why the research is essential (vaccines, diseases that have been wiped out).
• Conclusion: your opinion, clearly.

Use: 2 phrasal verbs from today · 1 Present Perfect (Scientists have developed…) · 1 Past Perfect (Before vaccines had been invented, …).
